# Discussion {#sec-discussion .deo-discussion}

This review asked what citizen involvement looks like at each stage of research,
and which initiatives, in Indonesia and elsewhere, have put it into practice.
Across eight cases, citizens held leading roles at every stage only where the
group that founded the initiative led the work: the Patient-Led Research
Collaborative and LaporCovid-19. In those two cases, involvement changed the
research question and produced evidence before official or conventional sources
did. In the other six cases, citizen roles were mostly limited to data
collection and to consultation on selected components. In the two failures, the
people whose data were used had no research role at all. No item was met in
six or more of the eight cases, and twelve of the eighteen items were met in two
or fewer. The most consistently lacking practices were returning results to
participants, letting contributors choose their credit, evaluating the project,
opening data and results, and documenting consent and ethics review. For most of
these, the sources simply did not say. These findings are consistent with the
systematic review of citizen science in mental health. That review found that
citizen scientists contributed mostly through data collection, and that
feedback, data availability and attribution were rarely reported
[@todowede2023].

Citizen leadership and uptake did not go together. The two founder-led cases
changed which questions were asked, but documented use of their findings by
decision-makers was partial. LaporCovid-19's data challenged official figures,
and its relationship with government stayed contested [@laporcovid2021].
Findings from the Patient-Led Research Collaborative drew attention, but the
sources we reviewed document no route into decisions. The only case with
documented uptake was the Indonesian Red Cross community-based surveillance. It
was designed with government stakeholders and built into the national
early-warning system and local budgets [@ifrc2021]. Its volunteers, however,
reported to a protocol designed by others and had no role in analysis. Both failures began with an
organisation acting on behalf of people in distress without asking them. With
one clear success among eight purposively chosen cases, we cannot say what
produces uptake. The pattern does raise a practical question: how can citizen
leadership over the question be combined with the institutional routes through
which findings become policy or programmes? The cases point to three conditions
that may bear on this question, and we set them out in the next paragraphs. We
offer them as conditions suggested by the cases, not as tested findings.

The first condition is a pathway from findings to decisions, agreed at the design
stage with a named institutional counterpart. In the Red Cross case the
counterpart was part of the design: alerts fed into the national early-warning
system, and local governments took ownership, with Boyolali prioritising the
programme in its budget [@ifrc2021]. CoAct shows the weaker version. Its
assembly produced 14 recommendations and public commitments from a city
councillor and the director of the National Mental Health Pact, yet we could
trace no adoption [@ub2022assembly; @bcn2023plan], which suggests that
commitments need to be recorded and followed up. Youth-GEMS states openly where
young people's involvement stops and why [@youthgems_decisions2025], a clear
role agreement that institutions can accept. In LaporCovid-19, the health-worker
database was built with professional associations, a news organisation and a
research unit, and the analysis had Ministry of Health ethics approval
[@ekawati2022]. This is a single observation, but it shows that a civil-society
database can gain institutional standing without being run by an institution.
Wider evidence points the same way, with caution. A systematic review of 145
studies found that collaboration and relationships between researchers and
policymakers were among the most often reported facilitators of evidence use,
and that poor access to relevant research and research arriving too late were
the main barriers [@oliver2014]. A scoping review of integrated knowledge
translation, in which research is done in partnership with decision-makers from
the outset, found that most evaluated partnerships reported at least one
positive outcome, but it is not known which partnership strategies lead to which
outcomes [@gagliardi2016]. In Indonesia, a ministerial regulation already
defines community-based surveillance and how volunteers are recruited and
organised at village level, but it covers zoonoses and emerging infectious
diseases only [@permenkopmk7_2022]. We cite it as an analogy for what a pathway
could look like, not as a legal basis for mental-health reporting.

A benchmark outside our eight cases is the NIH RECOVER programme on Long COVID.
The protocol of its adult cohort states that patient representatives give input
on all study processes, and some were recruited from advocacy groups including
the Patient-Led Research Collaborative [@horwitz2023]; representatives have
described the partnership from their side [@kim2023]. Embedding patients in a
research programme is not the same as institutions using findings that patients
generated (item C3), and the depth of embedding is open to question. A survey of
members of RECOVER's clinical-trial protocol working groups found that most
patient, caregiver and community representatives felt their input was valued,
but gaps in role clarity, communication and integration of feedback persisted
[@leverty2026]. We found no peer-reviewed account of the policy influence of the
Collaborative's survey. A news feature in *Nature*, which is journalism and not
peer-reviewed evidence, reported that the survey had been mentioned in some 60
policy statements and that patient-led efforts had helped to shape research
programmes [@fairbank2024]. Taken together, the benchmark suggests that
influence on research design and on policy discussion is achievable, while
decision-makers' use of findings is harder to show.

The second condition is legitimacy, and both failures broke down at consent. In
the Crisis Text Line case, data given in crisis under a terms-of-service link
were later licensed for a commercial purpose [@eysenbach2025]. In Samaritans
Radar, people were monitored without knowing it, under an opt-out design
[@responsibledata_radar]. Both activities were discredited and ended under
public pressure. A similar loss of public trust ended England's national
plan to share general-practice records, which proceeded without what has been
called a "social licence" [@carter2015]. Positive approaches exist. The MindKind
study asked young people in India, South Africa and the United Kingdom how their
mental-health data should be governed, and found that they held strong
preferences about who should access their data and were willing to help design
more open data-sharing arrangements [@mindkind2022]. In Indonesia, personal data
protection is regulated by Law 27/2022 [@uupdp2022], and the Health Law of 2023
contains provisions on health information systems [@uu17_2023]; we cite both at
a general level and do not analyse their provisions here. Together, these cases
suggest that consent for mental-health data should be specific to each study,
recorded so that it can be checked, renewed when the purpose changes, and opt-in
by default. These requirements are developed as principles in Paper 2 of this
series.

The third condition is credibility, which depends on being able to see how a
project was run. Most of the consistently lacking items were unreported rather
than shown to be absent, so from public sources we cannot tell whether projects
failed to return results or simply did not write about it. The same gap was
found in the mental-health citizen science literature [@todowede2023]. Reporting
guidance already exists: the GRIPP2 checklists describe how to report patient
and public involvement [@staniszewska2017], and the systematic review proposed
mental-health-specific reporting recommendations for each ECSA principle
[@todowede2023]. Our 18 items could serve as a complementary checklist, allowing
projects to state explicitly which practices they followed, including whether
they evaluated themselves. Reporting also needs to say whose experience is
represented. Typologies of participation, from Arnstein's ladder [@arnstein1969]
to Haklay's levels [@haklay2013], rank projects by how much power citizens hold.
They do not distinguish which citizens hold it. In LaporCovid-19, the leading
roles were held by a coalition of experts, journalists and activists while lay
members of the public mainly reported data [@rinaldi2024; @ekawati2022]; the
Patient-Led Research Collaborative was led by people with Long COVID who
describe themselves as patient-researchers [@mccorkell2021; @fitzgerald2024]. If
participation is dominated by a small or well-connected group, it risks the
"elite capture" described in lived-experience research [@okoroji2023], and the
people most affected by distress, who may have the least time, energy and
confidence to take part, remain unheard. Future frameworks should record not
only the level of participation but also whose experience is represented at each
level.

For Indonesia, the three conditions translate into a design sequence for
citizen-centred research on stress, depression, anxiety, burnout and
resilience. We offer it as a recommendation for future practice to be tested,
not as something these eight cases have shown to work:

1. Citizens help choose the question. Indonesian respondents named community
   support, including mental support, as a way they wanted to contribute
   [@tan2024].
2. A named institutional counterpart and a pathway for using findings are agreed
   before data collection starts.
3. Consent is opt-in, specific to the study and recorded.
4. Results go back to participants in a usable form.
5. Volunteers are trained, supported and retained.
6. The study is evaluated and reported against the 18 items.

Indonesia already has parts of this to learn from, with clear limits. Lay mental
health cadres (*kader kesehatan jiwa*) work with community health centres; in a
qualitative study of 71 cadres in four provinces they described sorting
residents by risk, visiting homes, referring people to care and supporting
families with medication [@susanti2024]. Evaluations of cadre training report
gains in cadres' self-efficacy and skills [@sutarjo2016] and in knowledge
[@marastuti2020], but we found no evaluation that measured outcomes for patients
or communities. These benchmarks show that a cadre channel exists and can be
trained, not that it improves health. Volunteer support is the weak point.
In Sleman, village governments paid community health volunteers IDR 300,000 to
450,000 per year regardless of performance, and newer programmes, including
mental health, had no incentive at all [@sitorukmi2025]; in Malang, cadres
received about IDR 25,000 to 50,000 per month, set by the village government
[@gadsden2021; @gadsden2022]; and mental health cadres in four provinces reported
irregular payments [@susanti2024]. These are local examples and not national
figures, and none of the studies measured retention. The unpaid Red Cross
volunteers were retained at 73% (171 of 234), and the report names retention as
a challenge [@ifrc2021]. As a regional comparator for sustaining volunteer
systems, Thailand's village health volunteer programme is long-running and
integrated with government [@kowitt2015], and its volunteers carried out
community surveillance during COVID-19 [@kaweenuttayanon2021]. The wider
Indonesian context fits steps 2 to 4. Most Indonesian respondents had never heard
of citizen science, but most owned a smartphone and had internet access
[@tan2024]; during the pandemic, grassroots groups published data because
official information was inadequate [@nadzir2020]; and community members said
they did not know how the information they gave was used [@kumar2025]. A clear
pathway, specific consent and feedback to participants could help address
each of these, although that remains to be tested.

The next steps fall into this series and into wider research. Within the series,
Paper 2 turns the consent and reporting lessons into principles for
research-ready health data, Paper 3 assesses an open-source research platform
against those principles, and Paper 4 is a baseline study of depression,
anxiety, burnout, resilience and functioning among adults in three Indonesian
cities. Beyond the series, four gaps stand out. The scoring framework needs to
be validated, including agreement between independent raters. Interviews with
project teams would show whether the practices scored as not reported took
place. The cadre programmes need evaluations that measure outcomes for patients
and communities. And a mental-health pilot in Indonesia, with a pre-agreed
pathway to a named institution and a way to track commitments, would test
whether the design sequence above makes findings actionable.

## Strengths and limitations

This review has three strengths. All cases were scored on a common framework
with rules fixed before scoring, by two coders. Failure cases were
included and scored on the same terms as successes. And the review includes
cases from a middle-income country, addressing a gap in the existing evidence
[@todowede2023].

It also has limitations. First, it relies on public documents, so practices
that were not reported could not be scored; the high number of `NR` scores
reflects this. Second, the cases were selected purposively and are not
representative of citizen science in mental health. Third, the evidence for
some cases rests on organisational reports, project websites or news, which may
present projects favourably or selectively. Fourth, the scoring framework is
new and has not been validated beyond this review. Fifth, the unit of analysis
and definition of a citizen required judgement, particularly for failure cases
in which people whose data were used had no research role. Finally, the lead
author founded a company that develops a research platform evaluated later in
this series; the steps taken to limit bias are described in the Methods and
Declarations. In addition, the D1 score for LaporCovid-19 was changed from not
reported to partly met after a follow-up search on 16 November 2026, and rests on
organisational sources. Finally, we found no Indonesian citizen science project
focused on mental health, which may reflect a true absence or limits of our
search; this is why the Indonesian recommendations above draw on benchmarks from
other fields and countries.
